newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S. faces terrorist threat, trade setback, at APEC.
newsitem.headline: U.S. faces terrorist threat, trade setback, at APEC.

text.p: Threats of terrorist attack and efforts to blunt its free trade drive put the United States on the defensive on Friday as it prepared for the APEC summit.
U.S. officials had hoped the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Monday would give ringing endorsement to their plan to slash to zero tariffs on computers and parts by 2000.
But Asian objections mean they will have to settle for less when leaders of 18 APEC economies meet in the former U.S. naval base of Subic Bay -- for years the main symbol of American power in Asia.
Aggravating the concerns, a U.S. official warned Americans they might be targets of terrorist attack in the Philippines.

Security sources said police were worried leftist groups may be planning bombings and assassinations to disrupt the summit, to be attended by U.S. President Bill Clinton, Chinese President Jiang Zemin and other key leaders.
And an intelligence report obtained by Reuters indicated explosives found at Manila's airport on Wednesday were not part of a security drill, as reported at the time, but a real bomb.

Philippine President Fidel Ramos, whose zeal for free trade has transformed his nation from "sick man of Asia" to Asian tiger, urged 450 top businessmen from APEC nations to "go, go, go" for a borderless economy circling the Pacific.
He was drumming up private sector enthusiasm for an APEC organisation widely criticised for being an empty talking shop instead of a force for global trade liberalisation.

The U.S. plan for open trade in information equipment, a key area of Asia-Pacific commerce, was seen as a test of APEC's ability to pull together and stamp its mark on the World Trade Organisation, which will hold its first ministerial meeting next month in Singapore.
Despite an appeal by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, APEC ministers managed only a watered-down general statement of support and agreed to shelve contentious issues.
Malaysia and some other developing countries object to the tariff targets and timeframes in the pact, saying APEC must move forward by agreement rather than by coercion.
U.S. officials made clear they would continue to fight to liberalise trade in an industry worth an annual $1.8 trillion and dominated by U.S. suppliers.
Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said that information technology products would be to the 21st century "what roads and bridges were to the 19th century".
"We must keep pace with infrastructure requirements of the 21st century and we must in that sense put our money where our mouth is," she told.
APEC foreign and economic ministers at the start of a two-day meeting agreed on an action plan that weaves together free-market initiatives by member economies.
The Manila Action Plan will act as a road map for the APEC goal of fully open markets by 2020.
At the same time, ministers discussed economic and technical cooperation in areas such as capital markets, infrastructure and education.
The ministers also agreed to refine the criteria for new members to APEC.
"New members will be announced in Kuala Lumpur in 1998 and will be admitted and participate in New Zealand in 1999," said Philippine foreign ministry undersecretary Rodolfo Severino.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), six of whose members are in APEC, has been pushing for quick admittance for the other ASEAN member, Vietnam.

Severino said 11 nations -- including Vietnam, India, Pakistan, Russia, Colombia, Peru, Ecuador and Mongolia -- had experessed interest in joining. But some members, including the United States, were opposed to rapid expansion.
As Ramos addressed business executives, baton-wielding police chased off students waving banners declaring "No to APEC".

Hundreds of demonstrators have been marching to denounce APEC's vision of a single trading bloc for goods and services. They say it will benefit big business and rich nations at the expense of the poor.
